headline: Hackers make French supermarket fridges too hot

sources.title: Hackers turn up the heat in refrigerators at hundreds of supermarkets in France, sparking fires and food losses (CBS News)
Hackers heat up hundreds of French supermarket fridges, causing fires and food loss (The Irish Times)
Hackers heat French supermarket fridges, sparking fires and spoiling food (The Globe and Mail)

chunks.text: Overnight from October 11 to October 12, 2026, hackers {{turned up}} the temperature in refrigerators and freezers at hundreds of supermarkets across France. In some stores, the temperature {{went up}} to 50 degrees Celsius, or 122 degrees Fahrenheit. The Paris [[prosecutor's office]] said the attack caused [[food losses]] and some fires. It called the attack "large-scale" and opened an [[investigation]].

verbs.correct: To make a machine's setting higher
verbs.wrong: To read the number on a screen
verbs.why: Can you turn up the heat in the car? She turned up the music for the party. Hackers turned up the temperature in fridges and freezers across France.

verbs.wrong: To be set by a worker
verbs.why: The price of milk went up last month. Her fever went up during the night. In some stores, the temperature went up to 50 degrees Celsius.

chunks.text: Several of France's biggest [[grocery chains]] said they were hit. One chain said 80 of its supermarkets were affected. The owner of another chain said refrigerators in about 150 of its stores stayed at 50 degrees for six hours. It said staff {{threw away}} all the affected food to avoid [[health risks]]. The head of that chain said losses across France could {{add up to}} tens of millions of euros in a single day.

verbs.correct: To remove something you do not want
verbs.wrong: To sell something at a low price
verbs.why: I threw away the old milk in the fridge. Please don't throw away those boxes yet. Staff threw away all the affected food to avoid health risks.
Small daily costs can add up to a lot of money. Her bills added up to 900 dollars this month. Losses across France could add up to tens of millions of euros in a single day.

chunks.text: A third chain said about 100 of its stores were [[targeted]]. Its head called the attack "[[unprecedented]]." News reports give different store numbers, and there is no [[official total]]. Investigators are still trying to {{find out}} who {{broke into}} the systems. France's prime minister ordered the national agency for computer security to {{look into}} the attack. According to his office, the agency found a [[weak spot]] in software from a Danish company that makes refrigerator [[control systems]].

verbs.correct: To learn a fact you did not know
verbs.wrong: To report a crime to the police
verbs.why: I called the bank to find out why my card stopped working. We found out the store was closed only when we got there. Investigators are still trying to find out who did the attack.

verbs.correct: To get inside a computer system illegally
verbs.wrong: To sell data from a computer system
verbs.why: Someone broke into my email account and sent strange messages. The bank said nobody broke into its computers. Investigators want to know who broke into the fridge systems.
The school will look into the problem with the heating. My manager promised to look into my complaint. The prime minister ordered the national agency for computer security to look into the attack.

chunks.text: The agency has {{reached out to}} the Danish company. The company said the affected units were running [[outdated]] software. It said it had told customers for years to [[update]] their systems. A security expert said store refrigerators were {{cut off}} from the internet for many years. Now many are linked through [[sensors]] or [[remote monitoring]]. A French retail group {{called for}} full [[transparency]] from the Danish company. The European Union's food commissioner {{spoke out against}} the attack. He said [[food security]] needs more attention.

verbs.wrong: To blame someone for a problem
verbs.why: Several customers reached out to the store about the problem. You can reach out to our help desk at any time. The national agency has reached out to the Danish company.

verbs.correct: To have no link to a network
verbs.wrong: To be run by an outside company
verbs.why: The island was cut off from the phone network for two days. Our office was cut off from the internet during the storm. Store fridges were cut off from the internet for many years.
Parents called for safer roads near the school. The workers called for higher pay. A French retail group called for full transparency from the Danish company.

verbs.correct: To publicly say you oppose something
verbs.wrong: To give a news report about something
verbs.why: Many doctors spoke out against the new rule. She spoke out against unfair pay at her company. The European Union's food commissioner spoke out against the attack.

mainIdea.s: Hackers made fridges and freezers too warm in hundreds of French supermarkets overnight. Stores lost large amounts of food, and officials are still investigating who did it.
mainIdea.why: Hackers turned up the temperature in hundreds of stores, and food was thrown away. Investigators are still trying to find out who did it.

mainIdea.s: Hackers made French supermarket fridges overheat, and police have already named the group responsible. They say the attackers wanted to push food prices higher in France.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the people behind the attack are still unknown. Investigators are still trying to find out who broke into the systems.

mainIdea.s: France has passed a new law that forces large supermarkets to give unsold food to charities. Big stores must now sign deals with local groups or pay a fine every year.
mainIdea.why: This story is about hackers who made store fridges overheat. Stores had to throw away fresh and frozen food after the attack.

lines.text: Did you see the news about the supermarkets in France?
Hackers {{turned up}} the temperature in fridges and freezers. In some stores it {{went up}} to 50 degrees Celsius.
That's hotter than a summer day. What about the food?
One chain said staff {{threw away}} all of it to stay safe.
[[What a waste]]. How much money are we talking about?
The head of that chain said losses could {{add up to}} tens of millions of euros.
Wow. Do they know who did it?
Not yet. Investigators are still trying to {{find out}} who {{broke into}} the systems.
How did the hackers do it?
A national agency is {{looking into}} that. It found a weak spot in software from a Danish company.
No. The company said a lot of it was outdated, and it had told stores to update it.
So some stores were [[behind the times]]. Old software on the internet is [[an accident waiting to happen]].
The agency has {{reached out to}} the company, and it is checking whether other businesses are at risk too.
Good. Those other businesses need a [[heads-up]].
Even the European Union's food commissioner {{spoke out against}} the attack.
[[It's a shame]]. People need that food.
